director.chapterArc: The chapter moves from the rhythmic, precise arithmetic of survival (snares) to a tense, physical confrontation with a husk where mechanics override fear, then shifts to an observational dread as strangers appear on the rail grade, ending in quiet resignation. The narrator must maintain Callie's internal logic throughout: cold calculation during action, sensory grounding during exposition.
director.restraintNote: The combat sequence (P0065-P0082) requires a staccato rhythm but no panic; it is physics, not horror. The ending (P0114-P0117) must land on the mother's command as an absolute fact of survival, not emotional pleading.

cues.delivery: Establish the rhythmic loop. Read 'six snares' with a metronomic cadence; this is Callie's internal arithmetic.
cues.from: Six snares, and six empty snares, and Callie reset all six before she let herself think about it.
cues.through: She did them in order going north up the ditch line, the way she always did, because doing them out of order was how you walked past one and lost the wire. The wire was the part that mattered. You could always find another stick. There were eleven feet of brass wire left in the tobacco tin in her coat, cut into six lengths, and when it was gone it was gone, and nobody between here and Meridian was going to sell her brass wire for what she had.
cues.reason: Sets the baseline of procedural survival.

cues.delivery: Shift to a slightly warmer but still measured tone for the mother's presence. The dialogue is dry; do not soften it.
cues.from: By the time she got back to the road the light had gone flat and yellow and her mother was awake, sitting up on the boards of the barrow with the blanket around her shoulders and her boots off, working her toes in the cold air like a woman with all day.
cues.reason: Introduces the relationship dynamic without melodrama.

cues.delivery: Maintain flat delivery for the mother's observation about clouds. The humor is dry and ironic.
cues.from: "I am in a tremendous mood. I've been lying on a plank looking at the sky since noon. I've had thoughts. I've had opinions about clouds." She got her boots back on, slowly, and she did the left one first and then sat a moment before she did the right one, and Callie watched her do it out of the corner of her eye and did not say anything about it. "The trouble with clouds is that they're extremely pleased with themselves."
cues.reason: Characterizes the mother as weary but sharp.

cues.delivery: Slow slightly on 'grade' and 'direction'. This is the pivot from observation to tactical analysis.
cues.from: She found the husk line an hour before dark, which was both the best and the worst time to find one.
cues.through: Husks went the way water went. That was the whole trick of them. They did not hunt across a country, they drifted through it, and they drifted in a line, and the line held for miles because nothing in them was capable of changing its mind. Find the line and you knew two things. You knew where they'd be. You also knew where they'd been, and a husk line four days old was a husk line you could walk down the middle of and sleep on.

cues.delivery: Read the arithmetic of 'One was money. Two was work.' with absolute clarity and weight.
cues.from: One husk was money. That was the arithmetic of her entire life since she was eleven, and it only ever worked in the one direction. One was money. Two was work. Four was the number that had killed her grandfather in a hayfield in the spring with a good tool in his hands and forty years of knowing better, because husks did not get cleverer when there were more of them and they did not get stronger. There were simply more of them, and it turned out that more of them was the same thing as harder, and nobody ever explained that to you in a way you believed until you were standing in it.
cues.through: The hook had come off the loading rail at the grain elevator in Thistle Ford, which had been her whole town, and which she had left in the spring and expected never to see again. It was a steel J about a foot around the curve, forged for swinging hundred-pound sacks, with a socket at the base where a wooden handle had been and a hole drilled through the socket for the pin. The wooden handle had broken in her first month on the road. She had replaced it with four feet of thin steel conduit pulled out of a wall, and a bolt through the pin hole, and a wing nut she had to keep an eye on.
cues.reason: Establishes the stakes through logic, not fear.

cues.delivery: Sharp articulation on 'stabbing a husk was like stabbing a wall'. This is technical instruction.
cues.from: She had spent an evening at Gaunt's Reach sharpening the inside of the curve on a wet stone, which was the part nobody thought to do, because a hook was for pulling and not for cutting. That was the point. You did not stab a husk. Stabbing a husk was like stabbing a wall — it went in, and the wall did not care, and now your arm was inside a wall.
cues.through: You opened a seam and you pulled.
cues.reason: Clarifies the physical mechanics of combat.

cues.delivery: Build a slight tension in the pacing as she prepares. The description of the culvert is precise.
cues.from: The culvert was the thing she had been hoping for since the moment she saw the fence go down, and she'd had to keep herself from walking too fast toward it.
cues.through: She took the mouth. She spent ten minutes on it before she made any noise at all, because ten minutes spent on the ground was worth more than anything she could do with her arms afterward. She kicked the silt shelf at the mouth into a step and packed it down with her heel so she had somewhere flat to plant her back foot. She found the two stubs of rebar standing out of the broken lip of the culvert crown and she took her coat off and she draped it over the higher one, so she'd know where it was without looking, because she had opened her own scalp on a piece of rebar at fourteen and she was not fourteen yet.
cues.reason: Sets the scene for the physical confrontation.

cues.delivery: Staccato rhythm. Short phrases on 'stones', 'grinding'. The action is mechanical.
cues.from: She heard it first as stones. Not footsteps — there was nothing in a husk's walk that sounded like a person choosing where to put a foot — just a steady grinding forward, loose rock rolling ahead of a weight that did not go around anything. Then it came out of the dusk into the cut and she could see it, and it was one, and she let out a breath she had not been holding on purpose.
cues.through: That was the whole thing. That was what the last ten minutes had bought her. It came in at speed and the crown of the culvert took it across the shoulders and it had to fold down into the opening, and in folding down it lost the one thing it actually had, which was all its weight going one direction at once.
cues.reason: Reflects the physical reality of the husk's approach.

cues.delivery: Sharp on 'down and back'. The action is a specific physical maneuver.
cues.from: She did not pull across. She pulled down and back, dropping her hips, using her whole body the way you did with a sack, and the sharpened inside of the curve went in and found the seam of the shoulder and took it. The arm came away from the trunk with a dry tearing sound, like a board pulled off a nail, and the ash came out of the seam in a grey puff and hung there.
cues.through: The husk kept coming. They always kept coming. They were not strong — that was the part it had taken her most of a season to actually believe, because it looked like it ought to be the other way around — they were only relentless, and relentless was worse, because strength runs out.
cues.reason: Highlights the technique over the violence.

cues.delivery: Maintain a breathless but controlled pace. 'Relentless was worse' should be delivered with factual weight.
cues.from: She was already moving — up off the step, out through the gap between the husk's bulk and the culvert wall, the space she had measured with her eyes before she made a sound.
cues.through: Outside, on the open ground, she got the hook back on her shoulder and turned and planted, and the husk was coming out of the culvert mouth already, down on three points now, faster on three than it had been on four, which was a thing about husks she had learned the hard way in a hayfield in the spring.
cues.reason: Reinforces the nature of the threat.

cues.delivery: Fast but clear. The description of the husk falling apart is physical and dry.
cues.from: It came. She stepped off the line — not back, across, the way you'd step out of the way of a cart — and put the hook over its back from the outside and pulled it into its own turn.
cues.through: It went over. It did not catch itself. It came apart while it was still going over, the whole grey shape of it letting go at once and from everywhere, the way a sack loses its bottom, and what had been a husk was a long smear of ash down the cut ground and a settling grey haze in the air.
cues.reason: Completes the combat sequence with clarity.

cues.delivery: Return to a slower, counting rhythm. 'Twenty-two seconds' is an internal assessment.
cues.from: "Twenty-two seconds," she said to nobody, because she had counted, because she always counted, and because twenty-two was not good. Eighteen was good.
cues.through: The ash was the whole reason.
cues.reason: Re-establishes the narrator's voice after action.

cues.delivery: Measured and explanatory. The description of ash is a survival fact.
cues.from: The ash did not blow away. That was the first thing anybody learned about it and the whole reason the trade existed. It came down out of the air and off the ground and went hunting for the low places, running down the camber of the cut the way water runs, pooling in the wheel ruts and the cracks and the long seam where the old concrete apron met the dirt. Where enough of it gathered it thickened and took a faint shine, like something wet that wasn't.
cues.reason: Grounds the world-building in sensory detail.

cues.delivery: Shift to a tense observation. The pacing slows as she counts the strangers.
cues.from: She was three hundred paces back down the road before she saw them.
cues.through: They were not moving. That was the part that got into her chest. People on a road at dusk were doing something — making camp, watering, arguing, walking. These four were standing in a line along the edge of the grade facing her direction, and they had been standing there long enough that one of the animals had put its head down to graze.
cues.reason: Introduces the external threat without panic.

cues.delivery: Quiet and direct. The mother's reading of Callie is a shared understanding.
cues.from: Her mother looked at her for a moment across the fire, and Callie let her, and kept her hands still, because her mother could read her the way she could read a ditch.
cues.through: "There were people on the rail grade."

cues.delivery: Final command. The mother's voice is tired but absolute.
cues.from: "Then we'll want the fire small," she said, "and we'll want you to eat something before you fall over, and we'll want to be off this road by first light."
cues.reason: Ends the chapter on a note of resolved tension.

pauses.after: Six snares, and six empty snares, and Callie reset all six before she let herself think about it.
And it was one trough. That was the whole of the decision, and Callie made it standing in the road with her hands in her pockets, and it took about as long as it took to say.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing on the decision to hunt alone.
Emphasis on the value of a single kill.

pauses.after: She had spent an evening at Gaunt's Reach sharpening the inside of the curve on a wet stone, which was the part nobody thought to do, because a hook was for pulling and not for cutting. That was the point. You did not stab a husk. Stabbing a husk was like stabbing a wall — it went in, and the wall did not care, and now your arm was inside a wall.

pauses.reason: Critical instruction; isolates 'stab' as wrong action.

pauses.after: Then she went thirty paces up the drainage and hammered the flat of the hook twice against the concrete, and walked back, and stood in the mouth of the culvert with her feet where she had put them.
pauses.reason: Pause before the action begins; builds anticipation.

pauses.before: She let it come to eleven paces.
pauses.reason: Prepares for the specific distance measurement.

pauses.after: She did not pull across. She pulled down and back, dropping her hips, using her whole body the way you did with a sack, and the sharpened inside of the curve went in and found the seam of the shoulder and took it. The arm came away from the trunk with a dry tearing sound, like a board pulled off a nail, and the ash came out of the seam in a grey puff and hung there.
pauses.reason: Completed thought on the kill mechanics.
Emphasis on the direction of force: 'down and back'.

pauses.after: Callie stood with the hook out at the end of her arms and breathed.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset; transition from action to reflection.

pauses.before: The ash did not blow away.
pauses.reason: Foundational world-building fact; isolates the behavior of ash.

pauses.after: It was the last of the light, the flat gold kind that came sideways and made everything to the west a silhouette and everything to the east unnaturally clear. And to the east, on the long spine of the old rail grade where it ran parallel to the road about half a mile off, there were people standing still.
pauses.reason: Completed thought on the visual of strangers.
Shift in focus from Callie's internal state to external threat.

pauses.after: Her mother looked at her for a moment across the fire, and Callie let her, and kept her hands still, because her mother could read her the way she could read a ditch.

Revealing the core conflict; isolates 'people' as a new variable.
